newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Cricket-Weakness exposed as Canty wallop Wgtn.
newsitem.headline: Cricket-Weakness exposed as Canty wallop Wgtn.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Jan 16 - Wellington captain Roger Twose admitted Wellington's weaknesses were exposed during Wednesday's dismal 123-run loss to Canterbury in the Shell Cup limited overs cricket final at the Basin Reserve, NZPA reports.
Responding to Canterbury's meagre total of 204 for seven wickets, Wellington were all out for 81 in the 34th over.
That paltry total is only succeeded in miserableness by the 66 they scored against Canterbury in the first round of this summer's competition, also at the Basin Reserve.
However, Twose didn't think the Wellington side choked.
"Canterbury bowled very well and they are a far better side than us on paper," he said.
"I don't think we played any reckless shots and I guess the TAB got it right," he said, referring to the odds which favoured Canterbury to win.
"I thought 204 was a reasonable total to chase.
"But there are areas of strengths and weaknesses in our side and I think they were exposed," he said.

Wellington played some outstanding cricket to reach the final, and twice beat Canterbury at Lancaster Park, but too often they got home through the batting efforts of one player in a game -- generally Phil Chandler, Jason Wells or Roger Twose.
They were the only players to manage a degree of consistency in their batting, although Scott Weenink managed one century and Robbie Kerr a half-century.
However that was the sum total of Wellington's excellence, and when a combination as powerful as Canterbury needs to be beaten in a final, all those resources had to fire.
They didn't, and Wellington paid a humiliating price.

Canterbury's players occasionally appeared under-awed during the qualifying rounds -- they have been to the Shell Cup final five times in the last six years -- but when the final came around the competitive fires were burning again and Wellington weren't in the hunt.
Even while pressured by the only two consistent bowlers, Gavin Larsen and Mark Jefferson, during the middle stages of the innings, Canterbury kept driving ahead.
Wellington, by comparison, looked to have hit a brick wall, ending up concussed and unable to think of what to do next.
While successful captain Lee Germon felt his side had enough runs on the pitch, he still needed his bowlers to make an early impact.
"We knew we could defend the total if we got early wickets.
"We knew also that Phil Chandler and Roger Twose were the key wickets. If we could do the job against them we would get right among Wellington," he said.
As it was Chandler repeated his first-over dismissal from the washed-out day on Tuesday to enter the sports trivia books by being the only player out twice in the one-day final for a duck.
Twose, despite a valiant approach in scoring 24, couldn't find the support to stick around with him.
At one stage Wellington was four wickets down for nine runs.
Germon said: "The pitch dried out a lot from Tuesday but I didn't expect it to slow up as much as it did.
"I think when a stroke player like Chris Cairns spends 77 balls scoring 42, it says something about the pitch," Germon said.
